danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Anatole Kuragin (fyrst Vasilijs søn) opholdt sig i Moskva, fordi hans far havde sendt ham væk fra Petersborg, hvor han brugte tyve tusind rubler om året kontant og derudover satte sig i gæld for lige så meget, som hans kreditorer krævede af faderen.

Faderen meddelte ham, at han nu for sidste gang ville betale halvdelen af hans gæld, men kun på betingelse af, at han tog til Moskva som adjudant hos øverstkommanderende — en post hans far havde skaffet ham — og endelig forsøgte at gøre et godt parti der. Han pegede ham i retning af fyrstinde Marja og Julie Karagina.

Anatole gik med til det og tog til Moskva, hvor han indlogerede sig hos Pierre. Pierre tog imod ham uvilligt i begyndelsen, men vænnede sig til ham med tiden, fulgte ham endda af og til på hans udskejelser og gav ham penge under dække af lån.

Som Sjinsjin havde bemærket, havde Anatole fra sin ankomst drejet hovedet på Moskvas damer, især fordi han ignorerede dem og åbenlyst foretrak sigøjnerpigerne og de franske skuespillerinder — den fornemste af dem, Mademoiselle George, sagdes han at have et intimt forhold til. Han havde aldrig forsømt en fest hos Danilov eller andre af Moskvas levemænd, drak hele nætter igennem og overgik alle andre, og var med til alle baller og selskaber i det bedste selskab. Der gik rygter om hans affærer med nogle af damerne, og han flirtede med enkelte af dem til ballerne. Men han løb ikke efter de ugifte piger, især ikke de rige arvinger, som for det meste var kedelige. Der var en særlig grund til det: han var allerede gift — et faktum, som kun hans nærmeste venner kendte til. Dengang, mens han var stationeret med sit regiment i Polen, havde en polsk godsejer af beskedne midler tvunget ham til at gifte sig med sin datter. Anatole havde meget hurtigt forladt sin kone, og mod en betaling, som han lovede at sende sin svigerfar, havde han arrangeret at kunne udgive sig for ungkarl.

Anatole var altid tilfreds med sin stilling, med sig selv og med andre. Han var instinktivt og igennem overbevist om, at det var umuligt for ham at leve anderledes, end han gjorde, og at han aldrig i sit liv havde gjort noget uanstændigt. Han var ude af stand til at overveje, hvordan hans handlinger kunne påvirke andre, eller hvad konsekvenserne af den ene eller anden handling kunne blive. Han var overbevist om, at ligesom en and er skabt til at leve i vand, sådan havde Gud skabt ham til at bruge tredive tusind rubler om året og altid indtage en fremtrædende plads i selskabet. Han troede så fast på det, at andre, der så på ham, også lod sig overbevise og hverken nægtede ham en ledende position i selskabet eller penge, som han lånte af hvem som helst og tydeligvis aldrig ville betale tilbage.

Han var ikke spiller — i hvert fald brød han sig ikke om at vinde. Han var ikke forfængelig. Han var ligeglad med, hvad folk tænkte om ham. Endnu mindre kunne han beskyldes for ambition. Mere end én gang havde han irriteret sin far ved at ødelægge sin egen karriere, og han lo af udmærkelser af enhver art. Han var ikke gerrig og afslog aldrig nogen, der bad ham om noget. Alt, hvad han brød sig om, var fornøjelser og kvinder, og da der efter hans opfattelse ikke var noget vanærende i disse tilbøjeligheder, og han var ude af stand til at overveje, hvad tilfredsstillelsen af hans lyster betød for andre, anså han sig oprigtigt for uangribelig, foragtede oprigtigt slyngler og dårlige mennesker og bar hovedet højt med rolig samvittighed.

Udsvævende mænd, disse mandlige Magdalener, har en hemmelig følelse af uskyld, der ligner den kvindelige Magdaleners, baseret på det samme håb om tilgivelse. »Alt skal tilgives hende, for hun elskede meget; og alt skal tilgives ham, for han nød meget.«

Dolokhov, som det år var dukket op igen i Moskva efter sin landsforvisning og sine persiske eventyr og levede et liv i luksus, spil og udsvævelser, omgikkes sin gamle petersborgske kammerat Kuragin og brugte ham til sine egne formål.

Anatole var oprigtigt glad for Dolokhov for hans kløgt og dristighed. Dolokhov, som havde brug for Anatole Kuragins navn, position og forbindelser som lokkemad for at trække rige unge mænd ind i sin spillekreds, udnyttede ham og morede sig på hans bekostning, uden at den anden mærkede det. Ud over den fordel, han fik af Anatole, var selve processen med at dominere en andens vilje i sig selv en fornøjelse, en vane og en nødvendighed for Dolokhov.

Natasja havde gjort et stærkt indtryk på Kuragin. Ved soupeeren efter operaen beskrev han for Dolokhov med en kenders mine hendes armes, skuldrenes, føddernes og hårets tiltrækningskraft og udtrykte sin hensigt om at gøre kur til hende. Anatole havde ingen forestilling om og var ude af stand til at overveje, hvad der kunne komme ud af et sådant kærlighedseventyr, ligesom han aldrig havde nogen forestilling om udfaldet af nogen af sine handlinger.
»Hun er førsteklasses, min kære ven, men ikke for os,« svarede Dolokhov.
»Jeg vil bede min søster invitere hende til middag,« sagde Anatole. »Hvad?«
»Du skulle hellere vente, til hun er gift...«
»Ved du, jeg tilbeder de unge piger, de mister hovedet med det samme,« fortsatte Anatole.
»Du er allerede blevet fanget én gang af en 'ung pige',« sagde Dolokhov, som kendte til Kuragins ægteskab. »Pas på!«
»Nå, det kan ikke ske to gange! Hvad?« sagde Anatole med et godmodigt grin.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Anatole Kuragin was staying in Moscow because his father had sent him away from Petersburg, where he had been spending twenty thousand rubles a year in cash, besides running up debts for just as much more, which his creditors demanded from his father.

His father informed him that he would pay half his debts for the last time, but only on condition that he went to Moscow as adjutant to the commander in chief — a post his father had obtained for him — and would at last try to make a good match there. He pointed him toward Princess Mary and Julie Karagina.

Anatole agreed and went to Moscow, where he moved in with Pierre. Pierre received him unwillingly at first, but got used to him after a while, sometimes even went with him on his wild nights out, and gave him money in the form of loans.

As Shinshin had noted, since his arrival Anatole had turned the heads of the Moscow ladies, especially because he ignored them and plainly preferred gypsy girls and French actresses — with the chief of whom, Mademoiselle George, he was said to be intimate. He had never missed a wild party at Danilov's or at the gatherings of other Moscow revelers, drank whole nights through, outdoing everyone else, and was at all the balls and parties of the best society. There was talk of his affairs with some of the ladies, and he flirted with a few of them at balls. But he didn't chase the unmarried girls, especially the rich heiresses who were mostly plain. There was a special reason for this, as he had gotten married two years before — a fact known only to his closest friends. While stationed with his regiment in Poland, a Polish landowner of modest means had forced him to marry his daughter. Anatole had very soon abandoned his wife and, in exchange for payments he agreed to send to his father-in-law, had arranged to pass himself off as a bachelor.

Anatole was always content with his situation, with himself, and with others. He was instinctively and thoroughly convinced that it was impossible for him to live otherwise than as he did, and that he had never in his life done anything wrong. He was incapable of considering how his actions might affect others or what the consequences might be. He was convinced that, just as a duck is made to live in water, God had made him such that he must spend thirty thousand rubles a year and always occupy a prominent position in society. He believed this so firmly that others, looking at him, were persuaded of it too and didn't refuse him either a leading place in society or money, which he borrowed from anyone and everyone and clearly would never repay.

He was not a gambler — at any rate he didn't care about winning. He was not vain. He didn't care what people thought of him. Still less could he be accused of ambition. More than once he had annoyed his father by ruining his own career, and he laughed at honors of all kinds. He wasn't stingy, and didn't refuse anyone who asked him. All he cared about was fun and women, and since in his view there was nothing dishonorable in these pursuits, and he was incapable of considering what indulging them cost others, he honestly considered himself blameless, sincerely despised rogues and bad people, and with a clear conscience carried his head high.

Rakes — those male Magdalenes — have a secret feeling of innocence similar to that of female Magdalenes, based on the same hope of forgiveness. "All will be forgiven her, for she loved much; and all will be forgiven him, for he enjoyed much."

Dolokhov, who had reappeared that year in Moscow after his exile and his Persian adventures, and was leading a life of luxury, gambling, and excess, reconnected with his old Petersburg comrade Kuragin and made use of him for his own ends.

Anatole was genuinely fond of Dolokhov for his cleverness and daring. Dolokhov, who needed Anatole Kuragin's name, position, and connections as bait to lure rich young men into his gambling circle, used him and amused himself at his expense without letting the other realize it. Apart from the advantage he gained from Anatole, the very process of dominating another's will was in itself a pleasure, a habit, and a necessity for Dolokhov.

Natasha had made a strong impression on Kuragin. At supper after the opera he described to Dolokhov with the air of a connoisseur the appeal of her arms, shoulders, feet, and hair, and declared his intention of pursuing her. Anatole had no idea and was incapable of imagining what might come of such a pursuit, as he never considered the outcome of any of his actions.
"She's first-rate, my dear fellow, but not for us," replied Dolokhov.
"I'll tell my sister to invite her to dinner," said Anatole. "Eh?"
"Better wait till she's married..."
"You know, I adore young girls — they lose their heads at once," Anatole went on.
"You've been caught once already by a 'young girl,'" said Dolokhov, who knew about Kuragin's marriage. "Watch out!"
"Well, that can't happen twice! Eh?" said Anatole, with a good-natured laugh.
